briefs.headline: NMDC targets Net Zero operational emissions by 2047
briefs.deck: The Net Zero roadmap has been divided into three phases – the short-term will cover FY 2026 to FY 2030, medium-term FY2030 to FY2040 and the long-term will run from FY 2040 to FY 2047
briefs.bodyText:
State-owned iron ore producer NMDC has identified energy efficiency, renewable energy integration, electrification of fleet, adoption of low-carbon fuels, Carbon Capture, Utilisation and Storage (CCUS) and demand-side management as the six key strategies as it eyes achieving Net Zero operational emissions by 2047.
The company has set an overall target of a minimum 90% reduction in operational emissions as part of its Net Zero pathway, with the remaining emissions to be addressed through offsetting measures as the roadmap progresses, NMDC said on Friday.
It said this announcing the company has set a target to achieve Net Zero operational emissions by 2047, covering Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions arising from direct fuel consumption and electricity consumption, respectively. It has decided to progressively reduce the carbon footprint of its operations and transition towards lower-carbon mining practices, NMDC said in a release.
Several initiatives aimed at increasing the share of renewable energy and reducing dependence on conventional energy sources have been undertaken, including a 10.5 MW wind energy facility in Chitradurga and solar power installations across its projects. Beyond Scope 1 and Scope 2, the company’s logistics infrastructure is also expected to contribute to the decarbonisation efforts. The upcoming slurry pipeline project is expected to provide a greener downstream transportation solution by reducing dependence on conventional transportation and associated warehousing requirements, it said.
NMDC also plans to increase the movement of iron ore through rail freight on the back of doubling of railway lines and other supply infrastructure being developed around its operations. Greater use of rail transportation is expected to help reduce the carbon intensity associated with the movement of minerals.
The Net Zero roadmap has been divided into three phases – the short-term will cover FY 2026 to FY 2030, medium-term FY2030 to FY2040 and the long-term will run from FY 2040 to FY 2047.

stories.headline: 'Haar nahi maanunga': Sujeet's Asian Games gold mission on the road to LA Olympics
stories.deck: Wrestler Sujeet Kalkal’s Olympic dream was shattered before he could even step on the mat at the Paris qualifiers. Stranded at Dubai airport for three days, he arrived in Kyrgyzstan after the weigh-in had ended. Now, the 23-year-old is looking at the Asian Games as a fresh start. Representing India in the competitive 65kg category, Sujeet is determined to win gold and keep his Olympic dream alive.
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: The last time Sujeet Kalkal came close to an Olympic dream, he never even got the chance to step on the mat.
Now, as he prepares for his maiden Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, the 23-year-old wrestler is looking at the continental event as the first major marker of a new Olympic journey - one that he hopes will eventually take him to Los Angeles in 2028.
“Asaan nahi tha, bhaisaab. Fir se start kiya hai, haar nahi maanunga. Olympics to sapna hai, poora karna hai bass [It wasn’t easy. I’ve started again, and I won’t give up. The Olympics is a dream, and I have to fulfil it, that’s all],” Sujeet told TimesofIndia.com ahead of the Asian Games.
There is reason for that confidence. Sujeet enters Aichi-Nagoya having established himself among the leading wrestlers in the 65kg category. He won the Asian Championships in Bishkek earlier this year and has continued to build his credentials in 2026. He also won the 65kg selection trials for the Senior World Championships in Lucknow last week, beating Anuj Kumar 8-3 in the final.
The Asian Games, however, will present a different test. Sujeet's 65kg category features some of the biggest names in Asian wrestling, including Japan's Olympic champion Kotaro Kiyooka.
Sujeet's competition starts from October 2, when the men's freestyle 65kg, 86kg and 125kg categories will be contested.
For Sujeet, the Asian Games is more than just another tournament. It is a fresh start for the wrestler from Imlota village in Haryana’s Bhiwani district.
“I was very happy to qualify [for the Asian Games] . It is a fresh start, and I will not disappoint. Behind this success is the hard work of my father, my coach and my entire team. I am in good form. I will come back with the gold medal,” Sujeet said.
“The 65kg category is a very challenging and competitive weight category. The world’s best wrestlers always compete in this category. But I have complete faith in my hard work and preparation. My entire focus is only on gold, brother. I have worked very hard,” he added.
It will also be a chance to measure how far he has travelled since April 2024, when a three-day ordeal at Dubai International Airport ended his first Olympic campaign before it had even begun.
Three days at Dubai Airport
It was April 2024. Sujeet was at Dubai International Airport, waiting to continue his journey to Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan, where he was scheduled to compete in the Asian Olympic Qualifying Tournament.
But record rainfall had caused floods in Dubai and badly disrupted air travel.
Sujeet was stranded at the airport. He could see water everywhere and could only pray that the situation would improve so he could travel to Bishkek, where the qualifiers were scheduled to take place.
Sujeet could only watch the time, calculate the days and hours on his fingers, and then sit back. His connecting flight was delayed and eventually remained stranded at the airport for three days.
A flight was finally arranged, but by the time he reached Kyrgyzstan and then the venue, it was one and a half hours after the weigh-in had been completed.
The Wrestling Federation of India and officials tried their best to find a way to get Sujeet into the competition. But the United World Wrestling rules left them with no option.
The opportunity was gone.
“I felt very bad. I have no words. It was four years of hard work, and it all ended in that one moment. I was in good form, and everything was over in a moment. I cried alone too, but I had faith in God. I explained things to myself and returned to India,” Sujeet said.
Father's words gave him strength
Sujeet returned to India devastated. At home, his father Dayanand was waiting for him. Dayanand, a former Greco-Roman wrestler, knew what his son was going through.
Sujeet immediately hugged his father. He became emotional and had his father's shoulder to cry on.
His father hugged him and told him: “Koi nahi beta, fir se mehnat karenge hum, Olympics khelna hai”.
Those words stayed with Sujeet.
‘I didn't give up'
Starting again was not easy, but Sujeet was adamant. He won gold at the United World Wrestling Ranking Series in Budapest in the men’s 65kg division at the start of 2025. He added two more gold medals to his tally in Zagreb and at the Tirana Grand Prix.
He then won a gold medal at the World U23 Championships in 2025 in Novi Sad, Serbia, followed by another gold at the Asian U23 Championships in Vung Tau, Vietnam.
He didn't stop there.
Sujeet became Asian Champion after winning gold in Bishkek, Kyrgyzstan. With that gold medal finish, he also rose to the No. 1 ranking in the world.
Now, he is set for his first Asian Games. A medal in Aichi-Nagoya would take him another step closer to his next big target - the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics.
“I didn't give up. I have worked very hard. I have to go a long way. If I had competed in Paris, I would have been 21. I am 23 now. I will be 25 when the Los Angeles Olympics comes around. Age makes a big difference. But I don't want to step back. My mindset is still the same — to win a medal for the country,” he said.
'Haanikarak baapu'
For Sujeet, wrestling was never just a sport. His father Dayanand, a former national wrestling champion who also represented India at the World Championships, introduced him to the sport at a very young age. Sujeet was just five when he was pushed into the 'akhaada'.
Dayanand could not go to the Olympics to represent India. Now, he wants his son to fulfil that unfulfilled dream.
“Papa is very strict," he says.
"Wo dangal mein haanikarak baapu they na, wo waise hi kuch hain (laughs). He told me, ‘Son, you have to become a wrestler. A wrestler’s son should be a wrestler.’ I have learnt a lot from him since childhood. He is both my guru and my father. Whatever I am today is because of him,” he said.
“His dream is to see me at the Olympics and see me win a medal. I will definitely fulfil this dream of my father,” Sujeet signed off.

stories.headline: Davis Cup: India trail Korea 0-2 as Nagal, Suresh squander early leads
stories.deck: Now India need to win all three matches on the final day to advance to the knockout stage which has happened only twice in India's history: in 2010 against Brazil at home and in 2018 against China in away tie
stories.bodyText:
India's hopes of making the Davis Cup Final 8 were pushed to the brink after Dhakshineswar Suresh and Sumit Nagal squandered promising starts to lose their respective singles, leaving the visitors trailing 0-2 against Korea at the end of the opening day of their Qualifier tie on Friday (September 18, 2026).
Dhakshineswar lost the first match of his fledgling Davis Cup career when Korea's number one player Soonwoo Kwon beat him 3-6 6-3 6-4. The onus to bring India back was on India number one Nagal but he also squandered a solid start to lose 6-2 4-6 5-7 to experienced Hyon Chung after battling for more than three hours.
Chung showed the temperament of a big player as he earned points when it mattered the most.
Kwon has not lost a Davis Cup match at home and that trend continued.
Now India need to win all three matches on the final day to advance to the knockout stage which has happened only twice in India's history: in 2010 against Brazil at home and in 2018 against China in away tie.
India had managed to erase 0-2 deficit to win those matches.
In those contests, legendary Leander Paes and Mahesh Bhupathi had pulled off the must-win doubles rubber and now N Sriram Balaji and Niki Poonacha have the huge responsibility to keep India alive.
Nagal was aggressive from the word go, going for his trademark inside-out forehands. Chung though struggled to contain his unforced errors, giving many free points to Nagal. The Indian got the kind of start he needed as he broke Chung in the first game.
The Korean handed a double break to Nagal when he hit a backhand wide, yet again his unforced errors benefitting the Indian, who raced to a 4-0 lead in no time.
Chung got one break back by converting break chance in game six, only to lose it once more.
Nagal squandered three points, two with double faults, and pocketed the opening set when Chung's return flew over the baseline.
After getting a measure of his rival, Chung found his rhythm, playing intelligent tennis. He kept moving on both flanks and after getting him pinned on backhand side, he would charge to the net for winners. He used drop shots effectively.
Game seven turned out to be a humdinger with two players engaging in 7 deuce points. Eventually Nagal took the game when Chung made consecutive backhand errors.
Nagal though dropped his own serve in the next game, serving a double fault at deuce and then netting a forehand. Set was locked 4-4.
Serving to stay in set, Nagal began with a long forehand. And Hyeon came up with a service return winner to make it 30-0. Chung earned the set point with an overhead volley winner and levelled the match when Nagal netted a backhand return after a long drawn rally.
Nagal trailed 1-3 in the final set after early break but fought to level it. At one-set all and 5-5, it was anybody's game and it was the Korean who walked away winner, with Nagal losing the steam and temper.
Earlier, Dhakshineswar made a confident start but could not sustain the momentum. He looked in control early on but Kwon raised his game like the top players do, leaving the Indian without answers.
Kwon changed tactics after the first set but Dhakshineswar could not respond as the Korean began to serve wide and on the backhand side of the Indian. His deep returns also did not allow Dhakshineswar to dictate the match as he was doing earlier. Kwon gradually found his range and didn't look back.
The low bounce occasionally troubled Dhakshineswar, particularly when he was forced to take the ball from an uncomfortable height. Kwon took advantage of a few loose shots, but a netted backhand and a return error handed the Indian the first set point.
Kwon saved it with a volley winner and then fended off another set point before holding to stay alive.
Dhakshineswar remained composed when the rallies were stretched and was prepared to stay in long exchanges. He eventually closed out the set with an ace.
Kwon responded strongly in the second set. He created two break points in fourth game, but Dhakshineswar saved the first with an ace and second with an overhead volley winner after countering a low lob. A double fault gave Kwon another opening, but the Indian escaped by pinning him to backhand side before producing a winner.
Kwon's pressure eventually told. Another low bounce caused Dhakshineswar problems as the game went to deuce. The Indian saved one break point with a stunning backhand winner, but Kwon converted the second chance with a backhand winner to lead 4-2.
The Korean then served big to move 5-2 ahead.
Dhakshineswar faced set point in the eighth game after netting a backhand, but Kwon sent the return just wide. The Indian then saved another set point with two consecutive aces after his forehand that sailed long.
Kwon raced to 40-0 while serving for the set and levelled the match when Dhakshineswar sent a return wide.
Dhakshineswar came under pressure immediately in the decider but held the opening game. Kwon responded by serving wide to make his opponent's returns difficult and held comfortably.
At 2-2, Dhakshineswar earned a chance when a Kwon return error brought up deuce, but the Korean responded with a sizzling winner. A well-executed drop shot took the game to a second deuce before Kwon held.
The crucial breakthrough came in the fifth game.
Dhakshineswar fell 0-40 down as Kwon's aggressive returning began to tell. The Indian saved the first two break points, but his forehand sailed long on the third to hand Korea a 3-2 lead.
Kwon consolidated effortlessly with an immaculate drop shot to make it 4-2. From there was it was one-way traffic.

stories.headline: Asian Games 2026: Quimcy Dsouza closes in on historic Teqball medal for India
stories.deck: She will take on Indonesia's Sumaya in the semifinals September 19 and a win will ensure the first-ever medal for India in Teqball - a dynamic sport, a combination of football and table tennis
stories.bodyText:
India's Quimcy Joaquim Dsouza is just a win away from securing a historic medal for the country in Teqball after marching into the women's singles semifinals at the Asian Games on Friday (September 18, 2026).
Making her Asian Games debut, Quimcy stunned top-seeded Yuina Sakamoto of Japan 2-1 (10-12 12-11 13-11) in her opening Group A match that lasted 43 minutes at the Nagoya City Higashi Sports Center.
The young Indian carried the momentum into her second group match and defeated Cambodia's Koemyean DY 2-0 (12-9 12-7) in 24 minutes to top her group and qualify for the semifinals.
Quimcy got a bye in the quarterfinals by virtue of topping her group.
She will take on Indonesia's Sumaya in the semifinals on Saturday (September 19, 2026) and a win will ensure the first-ever medal for India in Teqball, one of the six sports making its debut at the continental showpiece.
If the 24-year-old Indian loses in the last four match, she will still have a shot at a bronze on Sunday(September 20, 2026).
However, the Indian pair of Quimcy and Mohammed Anas Imran Beg lost in the quarterfinals of the mixed doubles event.
Quimcy and Beg lost 0-2 (7-12 10-12) against Vietnam's Hoang Minh Tan Nguyen and Gia Nghi Trinh in the quarterfinals.
But the Indians still have a chance to finish on the podium on Sunday (September 20, 2026), as they won the repechage tie.
The Indian duo started on a positive note defeating Philippines Jhoana Abulencia and Prince Augustin 2-0 (12-10 12-3) in their opening Group A tie before losing 1-2 (8-12 12-7 10-12) in the next match.
Quimcy and Beg suffered defeats in the next two ties as they lost 0-2 (3-12 8-12) against Cambodia's Thuonvireak Bun and Sophornraksmey Yorn before going down 0-2 (3-12 8-12) against the Thailand combination of Phakpong Dejaroen and Suphawadi Wongkhamchan.
But the Indian pair made a strong comeback to register a 2-0 (12-1 12-6) win over Salman Alebraheem and Hessah Alfailakawi to book a quarterfinal berth where they faltered.
In the repechage round, Quimcy and Beg got the better of Abulencia and Augustin for a second time in the day, beating the Filipino duo 2-0 (12-3 12-6) to stay in contention for a medal.
Teqball is one of the six sports alongside Mixed Martial Arts (MMA), Padel, Surfing, BMX Freestyle and Virtual Taekwondo which are making their debut in the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.
Teqball is a dynamic sport, a combination of football and table tennis. The game was invented by football enthusiasts Gabor Borsanyi, Gyorgy Gattyan, and Viktor Huszar in Hungary in 2014.
The first official Teqball World Championships was held in Budapest in 2017.
In Teqball, players use almost every part of their body except hands and arms to rally with a standard size five football across a curved table, divided by a transparent plexiglass.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026 | Time for India’s athletes to make it count
briefs.deck: The preparations are done, the hard yards put in as the country will aim to match or even better the record haul at the previous edition in Hangzhou
briefs.bodyText:
The number of athletes may have been reduced but India’s ambitions of flexing its sporting muscle at the continental level will be tested when the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games officially kickstart at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium here on Saturday (September 19, 2026).
The quadrennial event, which began in India and which the country hopes to host again in near future for the third time, will have 501 Indian athletes in 259 medal events across 36 disciplines competing for a total of 356 medals. With 106 medals in the previous edition, any hopes of getting anywhere close to it would mean a fifth of Indian athletes finishing on the podium.
The record haul in Hangzhou has raised expectations but the country would do well to add a tinge of reality to temper them. With an ambitious target of being in the top-10 in the medal tally by the 2036 Olympics, the performances at Aichi-Nagoya Games will provide both — a practical assessment of where Indian sports stands after the high of 2023 and a template for course correction to ensure the long-term targets remain feasible.
No one will be more in the spotlight than the track and field athletes and the shooters, who contributed almost half of the total medals in Hangzhou. Among the latter, Manu Bhaker — who along with shotputter Tajinderpal Singh Toor will be India’s flagbearers — on Saturday — will deservedly be the one to watch.
But there are others too, some bringing youth (Tillottam Sen and Ashi Chouksey in rifle and Esha Singh and Suruchi Phogat in pistol) and others experience (Rahi Sarnobat).
And then there are those that have both, the likes of Aishwary Pratap Singh Tomar and Anish Bhanwal leading this group.
The situation is same in athletics. With Neeraj Chopra out with injury, the mantle of doing the heavy lifting among the 74-member strong contingent will fall on the proven customers — Tejaswin Shankar, Murali Sreeshankar and Toor on the field. On the track, the return of Avinash Sable would be a welcome sight, the steeplechaser along with Gulveer Singh the biggest bet for a medal, even gold.
On the badminton court, P.V. Sindhu would be hoping for one last hurrah in her pursuit of a maiden Asiad title while Satwiksairaj Rankireddy and Chirag Shetty will be looking for more consistency after a topsy-turvy year so far in terms of results and injury concerns in their title defence.
Women boxers and compound archers are also expected to add to the medal count while Mirabai Chanu will be up against it in search of her first medal in the event, 12 years after her debut in Incheon and three years after a shock exit.
Among the teams, hockey will expectedly be the main attraction with tickets to LA28 at stake for both men and women. The recent outings at the World Cup is unlikely to have much impact, specially the men, who will only have to guard against complacency. For the women, China would be the biggest challenge but recent form gives hope.
Cricket will get the eyeballs, as it is bound to, but in terms of competition, there will be little by way of excitement unless either of the genders have a terrible day in their title defences.
The men, in particular, would be hoping to earn legitimacy for their title, given the final against Afghanistan in 2023 was declared on the basis of ranking after being washed out.
The men’s kabaddi team too will be itching to prove their win last time was not a fluke and put all the bad memories of a rancour-filled final against Iran to rest.
The preparations are done, the hard yards put in. It’s time to reap the results.

briefs.headline: Continental glory: On the Asian Games 2026
briefs.deck: India might get another 100-medal haul from a smaller contingent
briefs.bodyText:
Even as Japan, known for efficiency, welcomes its third Asian Games and the first in 32 years, on Saturday, the Aichi-Nagoya Games have already earned the ‘worst ever’ tag because of accommodation and logistical issues. A country that successfully hosted two Olympics — in 1964, within two decades of suffering atomic bombings, and in 2021, behind closed doors amid the unprecedented COVID-19 pandemic — is now strangely struggling to accommodate more than 17,000 athletes and officials from 45 nations in hotels, containers and a cruise ship. Despite these issues, 501 of India’s athletes, including 267 men and 234 women, across 36 disciplines, will try to keep its flag flying high. At the previous Hangzhou Asiad, India had an impressive tally of 106 medals and was placed fourth behind China, Japan and South Korea. There is a significant drop in the number of Indian athletes, from 650-plus in 40 disciplines three years ago, following rationalisation, discouraging a mad rush because of the perks and money associated with the Asiad. Nevertheless, Indian sports authorities expect around 100 medals, which may noticeably improve the athlete-to-medal ratio.
The presence of 310 debutants in the contingent signals a brighter future for the country, which has spent nearly ₹800 crore on Asian Games preparations in the last cycle. Shooting and athletics, which together field 105 athletes, should continue to be the major contributors to India’s medals tally, followed by archery, boxing, badminton, squash and wrestling. Stars including Manu Bhaker, Mirabai Chanu, Lovlina Borgohain, P.V. Sindhu, Aman Sehrawat, Tajinderpal Singh Toor, Gulveer Singh, Harmanpreet Singh, Smriti Mandhana and Jasprit Bumrah will lead India’s campaign. At 39, squash player Joshna Chinappa will be the first Indian to compete in seven consecutive Asian Games. The youngest athlete, 15-year-old cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, and the oldest, 55-year-old rider Shruti Vora, are the other attractions. Some attention will also be devoted to Indian men’s and women’s hockey teams, which will aim to win gold medals and secure berths at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. While India can take pride in fielding athletes in debut-making disciplines, such as mixed martial arts and teqball, it should ponder over its poor representation in swimming, gymnastics and cycling, which offer more medals and open avenues for Olympic glory. Meanwhile, the Indian men and women’s teams would be watched closely in cricket. In pushing for continental excellence, India should also remain vigilant about its deteriorating global reputation due to the sharply rising doping graph.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026: India’s medal record, medal-winning sports, and more
briefs.deck: The 20th edition of the Asian Games will begin from Saturday (September 19, 2026) in Japan. Here’s an overview of India’s past Games performances, the dominant countries and more.
briefs.bodyText:
As the 20th Asian Games approaches, Japan is set to welcome 15,000 athletes and team officials from 45 countries. India, too, will be sending around 500 athletes to compete in the Games, a win in which will do much to boost the country’s perception in the global stage ahead of its bid to host the 2036 Olympics.
Here is a look at how India has done so far, the sports disciplines that have given it the most medals, the established leaders in the Games, and when to catch the action for each sport.
India’s medal hauls
India won 106 medals in 2023, the highest since it began participating in the Asian Games. This came after a drop in the medal haul after 1982, when India won 57 medals. Then, from 2010 onwards, India has beat its previous Games haul, except in 2014.
Key sports events
Events within the athletics, shooting, archery and wrestling disciplines contributed the most to the total medal haul. Of the events that are not part of this year’s line-up, chess, roller skating and bridge contributed five medals in total.
Dominant countries
Besides increasing medals in recent years, India has also increased in rank with respect to other participating countries over the years. In 2023, it was ranked the fourth in terms of medal haul. On the other hand, China, South Korea and this year’s host Japan, have been in the top three over the past two decades. China, notably, has retained the number one rank throughout. Chinese Taipei and Bahrain have climbed up the ranks since 2002, going from the 8th to 6th rank and from the 19th to the 9th rank in 2023.
India’s Games schedule
Of the sports in which India is participating, teqball was the first to start. Rugy Sevens and Taekwondo are the last to start at the tail end of the Games on October 1. Athletics events of field and track games begin on September 24, and end on September 30. This will include events like the women’s heptathlon, men’s decathlon, relays, sprints and more. Shooting, another key sport, will begin on September 20.
Venues in Japan
For the Asian Games events, 54 venues have been selected to host. Most venues are located in the Aichi prefecture, with a couple more in Tokyo and Osaka.
Japan’s hosting has come under fire in recent days. One point of concern was the shoddy process in allocating accommodations to incoming athletes, with athletes detailing delays in getting their rooms and a lack of amenities during the intervening time.
Athletes were given either a container-style room or rooms aboard a cruise liner for their stay during the Games. However, these accommodations have been too cramped, with faulty amenities for some athletes.
Besides accommodations, South Korea’s National Olympic Committee had raised displeasure at the presence of a Japanese 16th century warlord in the Japanese group welcoming the arriving athletes. Japan and South Korea have a history of violence under Japan’s colonial rule in the Korean peninsula, with the warlord being known for his invasion into Korea.

briefs.headline: India set to lose Asian Games medal after Parveen’s suspension
briefs.bodyText:
Following boxer Parveen Hooda’s 22-month suspension for a whereabouts failure, India is set to lose a bronze medal in the Hangzhou Asian Games.
The International Testing Agency (ITA), the organisation responsible for results management, has confirmed Parveen’s suspension until July 16, 2025 for three whereabouts failures within a 12-month period as defined in article 2.4 of the International Boxing Association’s anti-doping rules.
“In addition to the period of ineligibility, the athlete’s results obtained between December 11, 2022 until May 17, 2024 are disqualified,” said ITA in a statement.
While confirming that Parveen would lose her Asian Games medal, Boxing Federation of India (BFI) secretary Hemanta Kalita said: “The ITA reduced her suspension by eight months, but cancelled her results during that period as well.”
The 2022 Asian Games was postponed due to Covid-19 and was held a year later, from September 23 to October 8, 2023.
Parveen, a 2022 Worlds bronze medallist in 63kg, landed a bronze medal in 57kg in Hangzhou and secured a quota place for the Paris Olympics. Now, she will lose her medal and the quota place and will not be eligible to participate in the Paris Olympics.
In effect, India’s medal collection in the Asian Games will come down from 107 to 106 without affecting the country’s fourth place finish.
The BFI has decided to field Jaismine Lamboria, a Commonwealth Games bronze medallist in 60kg, in the women’s 57kg in the last Olympic qualifier, starting in Bangkok from Friday, in its bid to reclaim the quota place. Jaismine will leave for Bangkok on Tuesday.

briefs.headline: I find GCL entertaining; it actually gives chess a new life: Abhimanyu Mishra
briefs.deck: In his maiden Global Chess League foray, the American chess prodigy was part of a side that finished sixth out of six. But the 17-year-old Grandmaster thinks highly of the star-studded, innovative competition. He talks about playing in India, his chess journey, and the strengths of reigning World champion Gukesh among others.
briefs.bodyText:
Abhimanyu Mishra became the world’s youngest Grandmaster at the age of 12 in 2021. He still has that record. He is also the youngest player to defeat a reigning World champion. Excerpts from an interview Abhimanyu gave The Hindu in Bengaluru, where he played for PBG Alaskan Knights in the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League:
How do you look back at your journey of becoming the youngest Grandmaster?
It was part of a bucket list. It was in the middle of the pandemic. Everything in the world had shut down, and I desperately wanted to break this record. I went eight months without playing any tournament. Me and my dad decided to take this insurmountable risk. I am not sure if I would take the same risk today. We went to a different country in the middle of a global pandemic, and if either of us got the virus, we would be admitted to a hospital. It would have been an absolute nightmare.
But despite all odds, we decided to take the risk. Taking the risk was one thing, but getting the title was another. I had a rating of about 2410 and no Grandmaster norms (a player needs three). I think I scored norms from two of the first three events, and after that I hit a dry streak. I had to hit the rating of 2500 for the Grandmaster title. I was missing the final norm narrowly. But I made it in cinematic style in the last tournament. I needed to win with black pieces against [India’s] Leon Mendonca, and I did. I was euphoric that this journey was finally over for me and my family.
You had another interesting game with Mendonca here at the GCL. From a winning position, you put your promoted queen on the wrong square, and he claimed it was an illegal move. The arbiter agreed, and you had to replay the move in one second, which was humanly impossible. And you lost on time...
We would have needed an F1 driver to make a move so fast. But I am okay with the claim made by Leon. It is what you do, especially in a team event, where every point matters. I would have done the same. I would do a lot worse actually.
Your thoughts on your maiden GCL?
I actually wanted to play last year, but it did not work out. I had some school obligations and some other stuff, so unfortunately I couldn’t play. I was determined to play this year. I had been following the GCL from the beginning and I found it entertaining. This is a very strong event. We have the world’s best players.
From the spectators’ point of view too, it is an exciting event. It is good to see the audience cheering for you from inside the venue. It actually gives chess a new life in some regard. I loved being part of my GCL team, PBG Alaskan Knights. We had [Viswanathan] Anand, who is one of the greatest players of all time. There was Arjun Erigaisi, who is very creative and an absolute madman. I love his creativity, and the way he can transform any game into a very sharp, complicated minefield.
Arjun also has the ability to take risks, and that is very important. He doesn’t mind being in a minus position, according to the computer, but as long as he is comfortable, he would go for anything. We also had in our team Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, who is very, very strong.
Your thoughts on the other prodigies of Indian chess – Gukesh, Praggnanandhaa and Nihal Sarin?
Gukesh has this ability to bounce back from very tough situations. Yes, his recent form hasn’t been good, but it happens sometimes. I am sure he will be back to his best. Pragg has had a phenomenal run of late, and he is mentally strong, like we saw recently in the Grand Chess Tour final against Fabiano Caruana. He was down by six points at one stage, but came back and won the match. Nihal is very tricky and does well in time scrambles. I have played with him a lot online and he is very, very strong in bullet chess.
You beat Gukesh at the Grand Swiss last year and became the youngest player to beat a defending World champion...
That was a very interesting game. Before the start, I realised I had two options. I was white, yes, so I could play something solid and I could try to press a little bit. But he is very strong, so it was unlikely I would be able to create real chances and win unless he made some very big mistakes.
The other choice was that I could view this game as a unique opportunity to create history. If I had lost that game, no one would have remembered, but it was an opportunity to beat the World champion.
That’s something I wanted to. So I decided to play the sharpest line in my repertoire (Bg5 in the Italian Game) but he has one of the world’s greatest opening preparations. He had come prepared for this, and I was thinking over the board, and I had this idea to sacrifice a piece. You are playing against the World champion, so sacrificing a piece is probably the last thing to do.
But I was trying to replicate what Arjun does in these scenarios. I mean, it was fine as long as I understood what I was doing in this position. During the Grand Swiss, I felt like I was sort of untouchable. I was in a very good state of mind, and it was like I would play my best chess.
If Gukesh wanted, he could have made a draw. But he desperately wanted to win. He has this hunger even after becoming World champion... he still wants to kill everybody. This is both a positive and negative trait, but I believe if you want to reach the very top, you need to be like this. You will lose games, but you will win more. In our game, he tried to do this, but it backfired, and I found some very accurate moves. I got to a rook ending, and then clearly converted my advantage.
There doesn’t seem to be as much support for chess in the United States as in a country like India...
Yes, it is quite difficult to be a full-time chess player in the USA. I don’t really have sponsors, but I am a very positive person. I hope things can still work. And yes, the Kasparov Chess Foundation has been supporting me.

briefs.bodyText:
The Asian Games chaos in Aichi-Nagoya continued ahead of the formal opening ceremony on Saturday (September 19, 2026), with the official welcome ceremony for several nations, including India, marred by disruptions, delays and confusion.

briefs.headline: Rags to riches – how Ollie Robinson plotted his way back from cricketing wilderness
briefs.deck: The 32-year-old pacer spent more than two years outside the England Test set-up, with his fitness, pace and attitude all under a cloud. However, in a stunning turnaround, the swing and seam exponent has come charging back, helping England win four Tests this summer, and three of them with Player-of-the-Match performances.
briefs.bodyText:
The official social media handle of the England and Wales Cricket Board recently crowned a ‘King’. Alongside videos celebrating his exploits, it declared – ‘New Ball King’.
Crowns, especially in England, are not handed out on a whim. They demand performances befitting royalty. This summer, one man has done just that, turning successive matches into his own royal procession – Ollie Robinson.
The road to royalty, however, has been anything but straightforward for the 32-year-old all-rounder. Before this summer, Robinson had last worn the England whites more than two years ago, against India in Ranchi in 2024, an outing where his returns were so meagre that he was banished from the English national cricketing scene.
Had it coming
The writing, though, had been on the wall for a while. Robinson’s fitness was a concern, dating back to the 2021-22 Ashes, before his back trouble resurfaced during the 2023 home season.
Then came Ranchi. A back spasm while batting was followed by 13 wicketless overs, with his pace at one stage dipping below 70mph. England had seen enough.
The then bowling coach Jon Lewis had made clear what Robinson needed to do. “If he’s going to perform consistently over a long period at this level, he’ll need to be a fitter bowler,” Lewis had said.
Robinson hardly helped his cause off the field either. During the same India tour, a podcast he hosted with his now spouse revealed behind-the-scenes details from the England camp, prompting the management to have the episode taken down.
While the England door remained firmly shut, Robinson went about rebuilding his career with Sussex. He helped the County earn promotion in 2024, and continued to pile up the wickets the following season. Significantly, by the start of 2026, Sussex had entrusted him with something England never thought he could handle – the role of a leader.
Elevated to red-ball captaincy, Robinson embraced it. Sussex won three of its opening five County Championship matches, while the skipper led from the front with 17 wickets and 305 runs. There was even a back-to-the-wall, unbeaten century at No. 10 against Surrey at The Oval.
Rekindling the fun
The transformation, however, was not merely about wickets and runs. A winter spent playing grade cricket for Sydney University in Australia in late 2025 had helped Robinson rediscover his love for the game.
“Just got the love of the game back, really,” Robinson said during his comeback Test at Lord’s versus New Zealand this June. “It’s only, probably, in the last few months that I’ve got the enjoyment back. And knuckled down a bit more.”
It was a long way from where his mind had been a few months earlier. Around Christmas, Robinson had virtually resigned himself to the possibility of his England chapter being over. “I thought at Christmas time I was never playing for England again,” he admitted.
But he knew that if there was to be another chance, there was only one way of earning it. “As much as I obviously want to play for England again, I need to take wickets and rip up trees to receive that call,” he told Wisden before the season.
And rip he did, with the ball, the bat and as a leader.
The then red-ball head coach Brendon McCullum certainly took note. “We said bang the door down, and through the weight of performance in County cricket he has banged the door down,” gushed the Kiwi.
Striking gold
At Lord’s against New Zealand, Robinson needed all of six balls to remind England what it had been missing.
The first two deliveries of his return passed without incident. The third trapped Devon Conway in front. Two balls later, Kane Williamson lobbed one to short-leg for a duck before Rachin Ravindra was pinned down for a leg-before. A triple-wicket maiden — some way to announce a comeback!
Robinson was not done yet. To his five for 39 in the first innings, he added two wickets in the second, and chipped in with a valuable 29 with the bat as England completed a 115-run victory.
He missed the next two Kiwi Tests, first owing to injury and the next because of non-selection. But the three Tests against Pakistan turned his comeback into a statement.
Robinson made the Dukes cherry swing, seam and dance both ways even as he used his height and high release-point to extract steep bounce. There was the wobble-seam delivery that would hold its line, the nip-backer that would dart in, and the full inswinger. Pakistan was left bamboozled.
England added another little twist to the plan — Jamie Smith standing up to the stumps to stop Pakistan batters from venturing on adventures down the pitch, allowing the seamer to keep attacking the stumps.
It began at Headingley with the very first ball of the series as Robinson trapped Azan Awais in front. His five for 51 was followed by three for 29 as England romped home by an innings and 103 runs.
Relentless
Lord’s brought no respite for Pakistan. Robinson’s first five-over spell cost just six runs before he returned for another seven overs that went for only four and fetched four wickets. Four for 11 in the first innings; another four in the second; England had the series in the bag. Three Tests into his return. Three Player-of-the-Match awards.
Edgbaston merely extended Pakistan’s torment. Robinson’s three for 15 in the first essay included his 100th Test wicket before he swapped ball for bat and cracked a 47-ball 50. Then, back with ball in hand, he removed Saim Ayub first delivery and Abdullah Shafique three balls later.
Pakistan eventually found a way to blunt him, but it was a little too late as England completed an eight-wicket victory and a 3-0 sweep. Robinson had 21 wickets from the three fixtures at a mind-boggling average of 8.76 and an economy rate of 2.04.
Numbers, though, told only half the story.
The 32-year-old’s skill was never under question. It was whether his body and mind could sustain the rigours of the highest level. McCullum had put it rather plainly: “When his pace drops to 75, 76mph and the threat diminishes, he is not the same bowler.”
There, perhaps, was the difference.
The Robinson who laboured through Ranchi at under 70mph had returned fitter, happier and clearer in the mind. The height and movement were the same. The control was still there. But now, he had the body to keep it all going. The result was 28 wickets from four Tests and England’s Test Player-of-the-Summer award.
There will be tougher examinations. The Dukes will refuse to dance to his tune sometimes; conditions will not always favour him; better batting line-ups will find ways to get runs off him.
But for a man who spent more than two years out in the cold, Robinson has certainly turned up the heat this summer. Nine months since that contemplative Christmas, he is now the No. 3 bowler in the world.
“The hard work’s not done yet. We’re just getting started,” said Robinson. More coronations in store? Time will tell.
